cls: Long-acting beta-2 adrenergic agonist (bronchodilator; available as transdermal patch and oral)
pharm: Selective beta-2 adrenoceptor agonist that stimulates airway smooth muscle beta-2 receptors, increasing intracellular cyclic AMP and producing bronchodilation; the transdermal patch provides slow, sustained absorption matched to overnight/early-morning bronchoconstriction.

summary: Tulobuterol is a long-acting selective beta-2 adrenergic agonist bronchodilator used for the relief of airflow obstruction in bronchial asthma, chronic bronchitis, and COPD. It is best known as a once-daily transdermal patch (developed and widely used in Japan and parts of Asia/Europe) whose controlled crystalline-reservoir release is designed to deliver peak plasma levels in the early morning, countering the typical nocturnal/early-morning dip in lung function. As a beta-2 agonist it can cause tremor, palpitations, tachycardia, and hypokalemia; like other long-acting beta-agonists, in asthma it should be used together with an inhaled corticosteroid and not as monotherapy. It is not FDA-approved in the United States.
indications: Relief of airway obstruction (bronchodilation) in bronchial asthma, chronic bronchitis, pulmonary emphysema, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Control of nocturnal/early-morning symptoms of obstructive airway disease (transdermal patch)

dosage.n: Apply to chest, back, or upper arm; rotate sites

dosage.d: 0.5 mg (0.5-3 yr), 1 mg (3-9 yr), 2 mg (>=9 yr) once daily
dosage.n: Per Japanese product strengths; dose by age/weight

dosage.d: Use with caution; consider lower dose

admin: Apply the transdermal patch once daily to clean, dry, intact skin of the chest, back, or upper arm
Rotate application sites to reduce local skin irritation
Press the patch firmly; replace at the same time each day (often applied at night for morning effect)
In asthma, use together with an inhaled corticosteroid - do not use as sole long-term therapy
Do not use as a reliever for acute bronchospasm; it has a slow onset
moa: Tulobuterol is a selective beta-2 adrenoceptor agonist. By stimulating beta-2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, it activates adenylyl cyclase, raising intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), which reduces intracellular calcium and relaxes airway smooth muscle to produce bronchodilation. It also inhibits release of bronchoconstrictor and inflammatory mediators from mast cells and may enhance mucociliary clearance. The transdermal patch uses a crystalline reservoir system that releases drug slowly so that plasma concentrations rise gradually and peak in the early morning hours, providing sustained 24-hour bronchodilation that counters the characteristic overnight worsening of airway obstruction.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to tulobuterol or other sympathomimetics
relative: Ischemic heart disease, arrhythmias, or tachyarrhythmia
Use as asthma monotherapy without an inhaled corticosteroid
monitor: Heart rate and rhythm; blood pressure
Asthma symptom control and reliever use
Local skin reaction at patch site

preg: There are limited data on use in pregnancy. Beta-2 agonists may affect the fetus and uterine activity; tulobuterol should be used in pregnancy only if the expected benefit clearly outweighs the potential risk, at the lowest effective dose.
lact: It is likely excreted in breast milk (as with other beta-agonists). Use with caution during breastfeeding and only if clearly needed; monitor the infant for irritability or tachycardia.
renal: Specific data in renal impairment are limited. Use with caution and consider a reduced dose, monitoring for systemic beta-agonist effects.
hepatic: Specific data in hepatic impairment are limited. Use with caution and monitor for enhanced or prolonged systemic effects, since the drug undergoes hepatic metabolism.

major: Other sympathomimetic/beta-agonist drugs - additive cardiovascular stimulation and arrhythmia risk
Non-selective beta-blockers - antagonize bronchodilation and may precipitate severe bronchospasm
moderate: Xanthines (theophylline), corticosteroids, and diuretics - additive hypokalemia
Drugs that prolong the QT interval - additive arrhythmia risk with beta-agonist-induced hypokalemia/tachycardia
Tricyclic antidepressants and MAO inhibitors - potentiate cardiovascular effects
minor: Catecholamine-depleting or other antihypertensive agents - altered cardiovascular response
interactions.food: Not relevant for the transdermal patch; oral forms may be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; limit alcohol during acute respiratory illness.
interactions.diagnostics: May lower serum potassium and raise blood glucose; can increase heart rate.

rare: Severe contact dermatitis at patch site

monitoring: Asthma/COPD symptom control and frequency of reliever use
Heart rate, rhythm, and blood pressure
Serum potassium, particularly with concurrent xanthines/diuretics/steroids
Blood glucose in patients with diabetes
counsel: Apply one patch once a day to clean, dry skin and change the site each day to prevent irritation
This is a controller, not a rescue medicine - keep using your reliever inhaler for sudden breathlessness
If you have asthma, keep using your steroid inhaler as well - do not rely on this alone
Tell your doctor if you notice a fast or irregular heartbeat, marked shakiness, or muscle cramps
Press the patch firmly; if it falls off, apply a new one and resume your usual timing
Mention any heart, thyroid, or diabetes conditions to your doctor
pk: Gradual (patch); designed for sustained effect, not acute relief
Plasma peak in the early morning hours (~8-12 h after evening patch application)
Approximately 3-4 hours (oral); patch gives prolonged sustained levels
Up to 24 hours of bronchodilation from a once-daily patch
Store patches at room temperature in the sealed pouch until use
pearls: Best known as a once-daily transdermal beta-2 agonist patch (developed in Japan) timed to cover early-morning bronchoconstriction
Long-acting beta-agonist - in asthma must be combined with an inhaled corticosteroid, not used as monotherapy
Not a rescue bronchodilator (slow onset) - patients still need a short-acting reliever
Class effects: tremor, tachycardia, palpitations, hypokalemia - monitor potassium with diuretics/xanthines/steroids
Rotate patch sites to limit contact dermatitis
Regulatory status: marketed in Japan, parts of Asia and Europe; not FDA-approved in the US - guidance from SmPC/Japanese package insert and beta-2 agonist class data
missed: If you forget to apply the daily patch, apply one as soon as you remember and then continue at your usual time the next day. If it is nearly time for the next patch, skip the missed one - do not wear two patches at once. For oral doses, skip a missed dose if the next is due soon and never double up.
overdose: Overdose produces exaggerated beta-agonist effects: marked tremor, tachycardia, palpitations, arrhythmias, hypertension or hypotension, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, headache, and agitation. Management: remove the patch immediately, provide supportive and symptomatic care, monitor cardiac rhythm and serum potassium, replace potassium as needed, and use a cardioselective beta-blocker cautiously for severe cardiac effects (with care in patients with bronchospasm).
